case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."

Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.
